investigations.question: After a follower successfully installs an InstallSnapshot whose last included entry is (index L, term T), must the follower accept the leader's next AppendEntries with PrevLogEntry=L and PrevLogTerm=T, and does it still do so when the follower already held a log entry at L from an earlier term?
investigations.hypothesis: installSnapshot sets lastApplied and lastSnapshot but never calls setLastLog nor invalidates the pre-existing log entry at L. getLastEntry returns (lastLogIndex,lastLogTerm) whenever lastLogIndex >= lastSnapshotIndex, so once the snapshot makes lastSnapshotIndex == L while the stale log entry keeps lastLogIndex == L, the tie is resolved in favour of the stale log term. The follower's PrevLogEntry==L check then compares the leader's snapshot term T against the stale term and answers Success=false with NoRetryBackoff=true. The leader sets nextIndex = max(min(nextIndex-1, resp.LastLog+1), 1), which lands on L; setPreviousLog(L) then needs the leader's own log entry L-1, which is absent once the leader has compacted up to its snapshot index (compactLogsWithTrailing can leave firstIndex > L-1), so replicateTo jumps to SEND_SNAP, re-sends the same snapshot, restores nextIndex=L+1, and the same rejection recurs.
investigations.discriminator: Drive one node with real RPCs: bootstrap it as a Nonvoter, seed a command at index 2 with an AppendEntries whose Term is 2, install an InstallSnapshot with LastLogIndex=2 and LastLogTerm=3, then send AppendEntries with PrevLogEntry=2/PrevLogTerm=3. The necessary property is met only if the last append succeeds; the suspicion holds if it fails while an otherwise identical control node without the seeded entry succeeds. Refuted if the post-snapshot append succeeds in both cases, or if getLastEntry reports the snapshot term for index 2.

open_gaps.question: Does the leader side actually restore the blocking state in one execution: with a leader whose log has been compacted so that the snapshot index L is at its head, does an unrepairable follower produce repeated InstallSnapshot attempts with no committed progress rather than converging after one snapshot?

latest_interpretation.rationale: Source establishes a necessary property and a mechanism that appears to violate it. Property: after a successful InstallSnapshot for (L,T), a node's state at L is the snapshot's, so the leader's next AppendEntries with PrevLogEntry=L/PrevLogTerm=T must be accepted. Mechanism: installSnapshot (raft.go 1814-1953) sets lastSnapshot=(L,T) but leaves lastLogIndex and any stale log entry at L untouched; getLastEntry (state.go 167-174) prefers the log term whenever lastLogIndex >= lastSnapshotIndex, i.e. precisely the tie produced when the follower already held an entry at L from an earlier term; appendEntries (raft.go 1475-1500) then reports Success=false, NoRetryBackoff=true. Leader side (replication.go 223, 256, 286-300, 370): nextIndex becomes L via max(min(nextIndex-1, resp.LastLog+1),1); setPreviousLog(L) requires the leader's entry L-1; once the leader has compacted past L (compactLogsWithTrailing can set firstIndex > L-1) that lookup returns ErrLogNotFound, which routes to SEND_SNAP and re-installs the same snapshot. Local construction feedback (harness assurance_generated_test.go, both sub-cases, run in a scratch copy) matched the prediction exactly: with the stale same-index entry, state_after_snapshot reported last_log_index=2/last_log_term=2 against last_snapshot_index=2/last_snapshot_term=3 and the follow-up append returned success=false/no_retry_backoff=true; without the seeded entry the same append returned success=true. That run is not a retained receipt, so the defect claim is left unresolved pending the controller's execution of the registered experiment; the leader-side loop of the gap above is likewise still unexecuted.
counterevidence: Behind-follower case does not trigger it: when the follower's lastLogIndex is below the snapshot index, getLastEntry returns the snapshot pair and the appended entries are accepted (observed as the harness control: last_log_index=1 < last_snapshot_index=2 -> success=true).

With the default TrailingLogs the leader normally retains entries below its snapshot index, so setPreviousLog(L) succeeds, the leader backs off one index and appendEntries truncates the conflicting suffix from its stored copy, converging without a snapshot loop; the loop needs the leader to have compacted up to or past L.
limitations: The retained execution has not yet run in the controller; conclusions rest on source plus non-retained local construction feedback.
The end-to-end repeated-snapshot cycle (the registered gap) was not executed; only the follower-side boundary rejection was observed, and the leader-side cycle is argued from source.

Reachability of the precondition through a full replica history was not exercised: the harness seeds the older-term entry at L with a legal AppendEntries from a term-2 leader, but a full multi-node history (old leader's uncommitted entry surviving while a new leader commits its own entry at L and compacts) is not driven.

investigations.question: With a leader whose retained log begins above its snapshot index L and a follower that keeps advertising an earlier term for L, does one execution show repeated InstallSnapshot attempts and persistent non-progress on that follower, or does the leader converge after one snapshot?
investigations.hypothesis: The follower rejects every AppendEntries whose PrevLogEntry is L (stale term from getLastEntry). The leader computes nextIndex = max(min(nextIndex-1, resp.LastLog+1), 1) = L, then setPreviousLog(L) needs the leader's own entry L-1; because the leader compacted up to its snapshot index, GetLog(L-1) returns ErrLogNotFound, replicateTo branches to SEND_SNAP, sendLatestSnapshot restores nextIndex = L+1, and the next append is rejected again. The cycle restores its own precondition and has no enabled repair, so the leader re-ships the snapshot repeatedly while the follower's applied index stays at L.
investigations.discriminator: Control peer and defect peer share one harness and differ only in whether an earlier-term entry occupies index L: one snapshot and applied index L+1 refute the suspicion; repeated InstallSnapshot calls together with an applied index pinned at L support it.

latest_interpretation.rationale: The compared predicate was that a leader with a compacted log must make progress for a behind follower instead of re-shipping its snapshot indefinitely. Parsed receipt CheckRun 7772ad1b5b154d498a27a79806bb0ea7: index 3 (loop_observe, defect sub-case) reports stale_index_entry=true, snapshot_index=8, install_snapshot_calls_early=2778, install_snapshot_calls_late=16207, follower_applied_index=8, follower_last_index=8, leader_last_index=9, leader_commit_index=9; index 1 (loop_observe, control sub-case) reports stale_index_entry=false, install_snapshot_calls_early=1, install_snapshot_calls_late=1, follower_applied_index=9, follower_last_index=9. Index 0 and 2 confirm both sub-cases reached the same leader snapshot at index 8, so the only difference is the peer's earlier-term entry at the snapshot index. Circumstances: legal trigger is AddVoter(server-B) on a leader whose retained log begins above snapshot index L=8; observation interval is 300 ms and 1500 ms after the call, under no injected faults, no partitions and a responsive transport. Repeated nonprogress: across that 1.2 s window the peer received roughly 13.4 thousand additional InstallSnapshot deliveries and its applied index did not move off the snapshot index at all. Stable mechanism: the follower answers PrevLogEntry=L with Success=false because getLastEntry still returns its earlier term for L; the leader rewinds nextIndex to max(min(nextIndex-1, resp.LastLog+1),1)=L; setPreviousLog(L) then needs the leader's entry L-1, which compaction removed, so setupAppendEntries returns ErrLogNotFound and replicateTo branches to SEND_SNAP; sendLatestSnapshot then sets nextIndex=L+1, so the next append carries PrevLogEntry=L again. Controls and competing causes: the control peer, identical except for the missing earlier-term entry at L, converged with exactly one snapshot, so the loop is not a property of single-voter leadership, AddVoter, or the snapshot machinery itself. Scoped defect claim: in hashicorp/raft fd2d6988362c434e9fda87b87c5fb0df, a follower that holds an earlier-term entry at the leader's snapshot index cannot be repaired by the leader; the leader's nextIndex/SEND_SNAP cycle restores its own blocking precondition and the follower makes no progress, so bounded liveness fails for that follower under the stated conditions.
counterevidence: The leader's own commit index still advanced to 9 in the defect sub-case, so the nonprogress is scoped to that follower's replication and applied index, not to the leader's commit index or to cluster-wide commit.
The same harness without the earlier-term entry at L converged after one snapshot, so this is not an artifact of compaction or of adding a voter in general.
limitations: The precondition was produced by a legal AppendEntries from a term-1 producer rather than by a complete multi-node history; whether one compatible history can legally leave an earlier-term entry at exactly the index where a later-term leader commits and snapshots remains the open reachability gap.

Only InmemTransport/InmemStore ran; the monotonic LogStore branch of installSnapshot (removeOldLogs) was not executed, although the follower-side stale term arises from lastLogIndex and is expected to persist there too.

The 13.4k figure is the observed InstallSnapshot delivery count for this in-process, backoff-free transport, not a production rate; the load-bearing observation is the count growing without any follower progress.
One peer, in one process, at one configuration (TrailingLogs=0). Whether the loop persists with default TrailingLogs once the leader has compacted past its snapshot index was not executed.

investigations.question: Does one legal multi-node history, built from real producers rather than a seeded RPC, actually reach the state in which a follower holds an earlier-term entry at the leader's snapshot index and then stays unrepairable, or do ordinary repair paths close the gap before the snapshot boundary is exercised?
investigations.hypothesis: A leader isolated from three of four peers can replicate uncommitted entries to exactly one follower; a successor elected by the remaining three commits its own entry at the first divergent index, snapshots there and compacts past it; on heal the follower should then reject PrevLogEntry at the snapshot index and the leader should fall into the snapshot loop. Local construction feedback did not show this: the follower converged with zero snapshot restores.
investigations.discriminator: Read the rejoin_observe event: restores_early/restores_late above zero with the follower's applied index pinned at the snapshot index supports the loop; restores at zero with the follower's applied index reaching the leader's applied index refutes it for this history.

latest_interpretation.rationale: Two things are recorded, neither of which is a defect claim. First, the retained run 5abe56ac189b467d8dd165fb90954406 ended with status error, exit code 1 and reason 'Package discovery, build or dependency preparation failed before selected tests'; its stderr shows './assurance_generated_test.go:91:2: undefined: caEvent' (also lines 136 and 147) and its observations file contains no events, so it carries no measurement and cannot support any conclusion - it is a harness defect on my side, not source evidence. Second, with the corrected self-contained harness the local construction feedback was consistent across two runs and shows the opposite of the suspicion for this history: divergent_prefix reported base_index 2, divergence_index 3, partitioned_leader_last_index 7, partner_last_index 7 and partner_store 1..7, so the follower really did hold earlier-term entries inside the successor's snapshot window; successor_snapshot reported snapshot_index 4, snapshot_term 3, successor_term 3, old_leader_term 2 and successor_store_first/last both 0, so the successor compacted its log away completely; rejoin_observe then reported restores_before/early/late all 0, partner_applied_index 4, partner_last_index 4 and partner_store 1..4, i.e. the follower's suffix above 4 was removed and it applied up to the successor's index without any InstallSnapshot being installed on it. The repair path is not explained by these observables: the successor's own log store was empty so it could not have served entries 3..4, yet the follower's FSM was never restored, so some other path must have reconciled the follower. That is left open rather than guessed at, and it is an important narrowing: for this legal history the precondition is reached but the follower does not remain unrepairable.
counterevidence: The follower converged in this history with zero FSM restores even though it held earlier-term entries at indices 3..7 while the successor snapshotted at 4, so an earlier-term entry at the snapshot index is not by itself sufficient to make a rejoining follower unrepairable.

The retained witness CheckRun 7772ad1b5b154d498a27a79806bb0ea7 remains valid on its own basis (single-voter leader with an emptied retained log plus a peer holding an earlier-term entry at the snapshot index) and is not addressed by this different configuration.
limitations: The corrected harness has not yet been executed by the controller; the numbers quoted are non-retained construction feedback from a scratch copy.

The repair path that closed the gap in this history is unidentified, so the negative result should not be read as evidence that the seeded witness is unreachable in general.

open_gaps.question: By which path did the diverged peer get reconciled in the executed five-node history, given that the term-3 successor's own log store was empty (first=last=0) so it could not serve entries 3..4, the peer's FSM was never restored, and the peer's final store is 1..4 with applied index 4? Candidate explanations that remain untested include an intervening election or leadership change, repair driven by a different node, and a path through AppendEntries that does not require the successor's log store.

latest_interpretation.rationale: The hypothesis for this investigation was that a legal multi-node history would leave a follower holding an earlier-term entry at the leader's snapshot index and then stay unrepairable, with the leader re-shipping the snapshot. The retained receipt contradicts that prediction, so the comparison is recorded as violated and the suspicion as refuted for this history. Parsed receipt CheckRun b9b56ddf3d7d43319db460b87846f71f: index 0 (divergent_prefix) shows base_index=2, divergence_index=3, partitioned_leader_last_index=6, partner_last_index=6, partner_store 1..6, partner_replicated_uncommitted=true, so the precondition really was produced by the leader's own AppendEntries rather than injected; index 1 (successor_snapshot) shows snapshot_index=4 inside the partner's stale suffix, snapshot_term=3 against old_leader_term=2, and successor_store_first/last both 0; index 2 (rejoin_observe) shows restores_before/early/late all 0 with partner_applied_index=4 equal to successor_applied_index=4 and partner_store 1..4. So the peer's suffix above 4 was discarded and the peer applied up to the successor's index without InstallSnapshot ever running on it, which is the opposite of the no-repair prediction. Consequential counterevidence and required narrowing: this defeats the premise that an earlier-term entry at the snapshot index is by itself sufficient for the leader-side loop; the loop I asserted earlier (investigation 542e6bce20cb456fb6a01a29002f7cc4-question-0, witness CheckRun 7772ad1b5b154d498a27a79806bb0ea7) must be read only within its executed basis - a single-peer configuration whose leader's retained log began above the snapshot index with no other reachable voter - and not as a general property of rejoining followers. That truncated basis is still a real, reproducible non-progress witness on its own conditions, but this receipt shows an enclosing repair exists in the five-node case, so the claim must not be generalised to normal multi-node clusters. The exact repair path is not identified by these observables and is registered as a necessary gap rather than guessed.
counterevidence: A legal history reached the intended precondition (partner holding term-2 entries at indices 3..6 while the term-3 successor snapshotted at index 4) yet the follower converged with zero snapshot restores, so the loop does not follow from the precondition alone.

The successor's log store was empty at the moment of healing (first=last=0), which is the strongest form of the condition my single-peer witness relied on, and still no snapshot was installed on the follower - so the enclosing protection is not compaction-related.
limitations: The repair path cannot be attributed from the emitted operands; the follower's convergence could involve a leadership change or another node that the harness did not instrument.

investigations.question: With a partition that truly seals the leader and one partner from the other three peers, does the legal history still reach the state in which the partner holds earlier-term entries at the successor's snapshot index, and does the partner then stay unrepairable?

latest_interpretation.rationale: This batch cannot link a receipt to a fixed experiment, so the conclusion is recorded as unresolved even though the corrected construction feedback is decisive and consistent. Answers to the open gaps: (a) gap about how the diverged peer was reconciled - it was never isolated, because the partition cut only leader<->majority links, so the partner accepted the successor's entries while the partition was in place and had already been repaired before the heal; sealing partner<->majority removes that repair entirely. (b) gap about which node supplied the repairing entries - the successor did, over the still-open partner link; once those links are cut, neither the successor (store 0/0 after compaction) nor any other node can replace the partner's suffix, and the follower installs the same snapshot about 700 times in ~1.3s while its advertised last index stays at 7 and its applied index stays at the snapshot index. Consequence for the finding: the asserted single-peer loop witness (CheckRun 7772ad1b5b154d498a27a79806bb0ea7) is no longer an isolated configuration - the same non-progress and snapshot re-send cycle is now reproduced by a legal five-node history in which the precondition was produced by real producers (the partitioned leader's own AppendEntries to the single partner) rather than seeded, and the earlier narrowing of that claim is withdrawn as an artifact of an incomplete partition. The retained five-node receipt CheckRun b9b56ddf3d7d43319db460b87846f71f is retained as a superseded harness result whose cause is now explained, not as counterevidence.
counterevidence: The superseded negative result (restores 0, partner store 1..4) is explained by the open partner<->majority links, so it no longer counts against the loop's reachability.
Reachability here is still shown by construction feedback rather than by a receipt in this batch; the corrected harness must be executed to make it evidence.
limitations: The corrected harness has not yet been executed by the controller; the numbers quoted are non-retained local runs (two consistent runs), so no measured conclusion is asserted.
One configuration only (five nodes, TrailingLogs=0, equal 1s timeouts, in-process transports); other settings such as default TrailingLogs were not sampled.
The harness still does not instrument RPC traffic, so the ~700 installs are counted through the follower FSM's Restore count rather than on the wire.

investigations.question: Is the snapshot-boundary loop caused specifically by the leader's compaction leaving its retained log above the index the follower's prev-log check needs, so that the identical history converges when the leader keeps a few trailing entries?

latest_interpretation.rationale: The predicate under test was that the outcome of this legal history does not depend on how much log the leader retains once it snapshots inside the follower's stale suffix: on that reading both cases should either converge or both should fail. Retained receipt CheckRun beca431464bf44ab9c3354145c21899f contradicts it, so the comparison is violated. The two cases share the partition, the uncommitted suffix, the snapshot index (4) and the observation window; the only difference is compaction depth. TrailingLogs=0: index 1 shows the precondition (partner_store 1..7, divergence_index 3), index 2 shows the successor's store fully compacted (first/last 0), and index 9 shows 687 to 697 InstallSnapshot installs with the partner's applied index pinned at 4 and its advertised last index stuck at 7. TrailingLogs=3: index 11 shows the same precondition, index 12 shows the successor retaining 2..4, and index 19 shows restores_before/early/late all 0 with the partner's applied and last index both at 4. Mechanism, matching the source: with the retained log starting above the index needed to rebuild the request, the leader's rewind to the snapshot boundary produces ErrLogNotFound, replicateTo branches to SEND_SNAP, and the re-installed snapshot restores nextIndex to the boundary again, so the same rejection recurs and the follower never advances; retaining even a few entries below the boundary lets the leader walk the prev-log index down into entries it still holds, the follower's conflicting suffix is truncated by ordinary AppendEntries, and no snapshot is transferred. Scoped defect claim: in hashicorp/raft fd2d6988362c434e9fda87b87c5fb0df, once a leader has compacted its log past the boundary a rejoining follower needs, that follower cannot be repaired - it repeatedly receives the whole snapshot while its applied index stays at the snapshot index - and this is a bounded-liveness failure for that follower under the stated conditions, with no enabled repair in the observed interval. This control also answers the outstanding reachability and cause gaps: the precondition is reached by real producers, and the failure requires compaction past the boundary rather than the partition or the snapshot alone.
counterevidence: With TrailingLogs=3 the identical history converges with zero snapshot installs, so compaction depth is load-bearing and the failure is not a property of the partition, the uncommitted suffix or the snapshot transfer by itself.
The follower's applied index and last index are pinned for the observed ~1.5 s; the claim is bounded to that interval plus the source-traced retry cycle, not a proof of infinite stalling.
limitations: Both cases used in-process InmemTransport/InmemStore and FileSnapshotStore, with equal 1 s timeouts; no network transport and no other timeout regime was sampled.
The default TrailingLogs (10240) was not sampled: it should delay the condition (the leader must extend that far past its snapshot index) rather than remove it, but that was not executed.
The exact retention threshold between 0 and 3 was not characterised, and the transfers are counted through the follower FSM's Restore count rather than on the wire.
One snapshot index and one five-node configuration; the number of installs (~700 per 1.5 s) is a property of this harness, not a production rate.
latest_interpretation.joint_history: Single receipt, both cases: indices 1/2/9 (TrailingLogs=0) and 11/12/19 (TrailingLogs=3) come from one execution of the registered two-case experiment on the same frozen snapshot; each case is a separate cluster built by the same harness, and the events carry trailing_logs so the cases are not conflated.

latest_interpretation.rationale: The lineage is now coherent and no claim rests on the superseded run. Sequence: the first five-node harness reported convergence with zero Restore calls and no snapshot install, which was read as ordinary repair closing the gap and used to narrow the leader-side loop; the sealed-partition rerun showed the loop with 668-697 installs and a pinned applied index; the paired control then showed that only compaction depth distinguishes loop from convergence (TrailingLogs=0 loops, TrailingLogs=3 converges), and the earlier run's cause was identified as an incomplete partition that left the partner reachable from the majority. investigations.question: At the moment a leader takes the snapshot that a rejoining follower needs, must the leader's log already extend TrailingLogs entries past the snapshot index for the boundary to be compacted away, and does the loop disappear whenever it does not?

latest_interpretation.rationale: The suspicion under test in this investigation was the generalisation that the snapshot-boundary loop occurs whenever a leader snapshots inside a rejoining follower's stale suffix, with a larger TrailingLogs merely delaying it. The retained receipt contradicts that reading, so the comparison is violated and that generalisation is refuted; the underlying defect remains asserted on its own, narrower basis. Parsed receipt CheckRun 0b99df9ed72e4cd2b653c5741e4eec3d, three cases of the same legal history: index 10 (TrailingLogs=0) rejoin_observe reports restores_before 0, restores_early 704, restores_late 715, partner_applied_index 4, partner_last_index 7, partner_store 5..7, successor_store 0/0, with the timeline at indices 4-9 rising 104, 219, 333, 458, 583, 704 and partner_applied_cmds fixed at 1; index 21 (TrailingLogs=10) reports restores 0 with partner_applied_index 24 and partner_last_index 24, and index 32 (TrailingLogs=25) the same, partner applied and last index 24. Indices 3 and 14/25 show why: after the snapshot at index 4 the successor's store was empty in the first case but 1..4 in the others, and the twenty post-snapshot entries left it at 1..24, i.e. no compaction reached the boundary. The arithmetic matches compactLogsWithTrailing: with lastLogIdx equal to the snapshot index at snapshot time, 4 <= 10 and 4 <= 25 make the function return without deleting, whereas TrailingLogs=0 lets the deletion reach index 4. Consequence for the record: the two asserted results (single-peer witness CheckRun 7772ad1b5b154d498a27a79806bb0ea7 and sealed-partition witness CheckRun f66fa4e4e0514f7e95b7788032144a30) are unaffected because both ran with TrailingLogs=0 and are scoped to that basis, but the claim must now be stated with its exact precondition: the loop requires the leader's log end to be at least TrailingLogs ahead of the snapshot index when the snapshot is taken, so the practical trigger is a snapshot taken while the applied index lags the log end by at least TrailingLogs (for example a user-triggered snapshot during a write backlog, or a threshold-triggered snapshot under sustained load), not a routine periodic snapshot in a caught-up cluster with default TrailingLogs.

investigations.question: Does the snapshot-boundary loop also occur with a non-zero TrailingLogs when the leader snapshots while its applied index lags the log end by at least TrailingLogs, i.e. is the narrowed precondition reachable through a threshold-triggered snapshot under a real write backlog?
investigations.hypothesis: Taking a snapshot at index L while the log end is at least TrailingLogs ahead of L makes compactLogsWithTrailing delete up to L, so the leader's retained log begins above L and the rejoining peer's stale entry at L cannot be reconciled except by repeated whole-snapshot transfers - the same cycle the TrailingLogs=0 witnesses show, but reached with a normal trailing configuration under backlog.
investigations.discriminator: Run the sealed-partition history with a small TrailingLogs and a leader that snapshots on its own while the FSM lags: the loop is supported if the peer's Restore count grows with its applied index pinned at the auto-snapshot index, and refuted if the peer converges to the leader's applied index with zero installs.

open_gaps.question: Which concrete harness produces a threshold-triggered snapshot whose index lags the log end by at least TrailingLogs, and does the peer then stay unrepairable? A local attempt with a 15 ms-per-apply FSM, SnapshotThreshold=5, SnapshotInterval=10 ms and TrailingLogs=2 failed to observe any leader snapshot inside its window, so the harness needs to establish the backlog explicitly (for example by driving many client applies faster than the FSM drains them, or by taking the snapshot while a known backlog exists) before any loop claim can be made for a non-zero trailing configuration.

latest_interpretation.rationale: No measurement is claimed. The source arithmetic recorded in the revised Behavior (0b99111e65eb4d9faae97028d6140ff5-knowledge-0, revision 2) says the boundary is compacted away only when lastLogIdx - trailingLogs >= snapshotIndex at the moment of the snapshot, and the measured three-case receipt (CheckRun 0b99df9ed72e4cd2b653c5741e4eec3d) confirms the converse for snapshots taken while the log end only marginally exceeds the snapshot index. What remains untested is the positive direction with TrailingLogs > 0: no execution yet shows a threshold-triggered snapshot under a genuine backlog producing the loop. The local attempt described in the gap is recorded as a failed harness, not as evidence: its precondition check (waiting for the leader's own snapshot index to become non-zero) never fired, so no event described a snapshot at all and nothing about the loop can be inferred from it. The asserted results therefore stay scoped exactly as before - TrailingLogs=0 with a snapshot taken at the log end (single-peer witness CheckRun 7772ad1b5b154d498a27a79806bb0ea7; sealed-partition witness CheckRun f66fa4e4e0514f7e95b7788032144a30; cause isolated by CheckRun beca431464bf44ab9c3354145c21899f) - and the practical-trigger question is left open for a harness that establishes the backlog deliberately.
counterevidence: The failed local attempt produced no observation, so it neither supports nor refutes the positive direction; it only shows that the chosen way of creating a backlog was inadequate.
Because the only measured trailing values that looped are 0, the finding must keep that value explicit in its scope until the backlog variant is executed.
limitations: No controller receipt exists for this investigation; the local attempt is construction feedback only and is reported as a failed harness.

investigations.question: Does the snapshot-boundary loop occur when a leader with non-zero TrailingLogs snapshots under a real backlog, i.e. when its retained log begins above the snapshot index, or does the peer still converge?

latest_interpretation.rationale: The prediction under test was that a leader with non-zero TrailingLogs which snapshots under a real backlog, so that its retained log begins above the snapshot index, will leave a rejoining peer unrepairable. The retained receipt contradicts it, so the comparison is violated and that prediction is refuted. Parsed CheckRun 62f089bd843641099558ff8d8831ab29: index 35 shows the successor's snapshot at index 4 with successor_store_first 5 and store_last 63, i.e. the snapshot boundary was compacted away while the log extended 59 entries beyond it; index 43 shows rejoin_observe with restores_before/early/late all 0, partner_applied_index 64 equal to successor_applied_index 64, and partner_store 61..62 against successor_store 63..64. So the peer was repaired without any InstallSnapshot even though the boundary was gone, which refutes the compaction condition as a sufficient trigger and shows the TrailingLogs=0 loop cannot be generalised by it. The remaining unexplained element is that the peer's store (61..62) differs from the leader's (63..64) at the same applied index 64, and the peer applied 61 commands, which is consistent with the peer snapshotting on its own during catch-up under the same small SnapshotThreshold; that confound is recorded as the next discriminator rather than assumed. Scope of the finding is therefore unchanged and must be presented strictly as: with TrailingLogs=0 and a snapshot taken at the log end (single-peer witness CheckRun 7772ad1b5b154d498a27a79806bb0ea7 and sealed-partition witness CheckRun f66fa4e4e0514f7e95b7788032144a30, cause isolated by CheckRun beca431464bf44ab9c3354145c21899f). No claim is made that a non-zero trailing configuration reproduces the loop.
counterevidence: In the retained backlog case the peer reached the leader's applied index with zero snapshot installs although the retained log began above the snapshot index, so the compaction condition is refuted as a sufficient trigger.

At the same applied index 64 the peer's store (61..62) differs from the leader's (63..64), so a store-bound comparison alone does not establish which node did what; the peer's own snapshotting is a plausible confound.
limitations: The backlog case shares the small SnapshotThreshold across all nodes, so the peer can snapshot on its own; the confound was not isolated.
The mechanism by which the peer was repaired in the backlog case is not identified from the recorded operands.

investigations.question: What remains asserted at the end of this run about the snapshot-boundary repair failure, on which retained bases, and which questions are still open?

latest_interpretation.rationale: State of this run. Asserted, each scoped to its executed basis: (1) a follower that has installed a snapshot for (L,T) but still advertises an earlier term for index L rejects the leader's next AppendEntries with PrevLogEntry=L/PrevLogTerm=T (retained CheckRun 72367650c8d0470d8197a7d2c0f97ce1, indices 5 and 6 against control 1 and 2); (2) with TrailingLogs=0 and a snapshot taken at the log end, the leader cannot repair such a follower - it re-sends the whole snapshot while the follower's applied index stays at the snapshot index (single-peer witness CheckRun 7772ad1b5b154d498a27a79806bb0ea7, indices 3 and 1; sealed-partition witness on a produced five-node history CheckRun f66fa4e4e0514f7e95b7788032144a30, indices 1, 2 and 9); (3) the load-bearing difference for the non-zero-TrailingLogs cases is how much of its log the leader retains below the snapshot index at snapshot time (control CheckRun beca431464bf44ab9c3354145c21899f, indices 9 and 19). Narrowed and partly refuted along the way: an earlier negative reading of the five-node history was an artifact of an incomplete partition and its Fact was revised in place; the generalisation that any non-zero TrailingLogs merely delays the loop was refuted (CheckRun 0b99df9ed72e4cd2b653c5741e4eec3d); and the further generalisation that the compacted-boundary condition is sufficient was refuted by the backlog case in the same receipt family (CheckRun 62f089bd843641099558ff8d8831ab29, indices 35 and 43). For a human reviewer the defensible statement is therefore: with TrailingLogs=0 and a snapshot taken at the log end, a rejoining follower can be unrepairable and the leader loops on whole-snapshot transfers; with non-zero TrailingLogs the executed histories converge, and the compaction condition does not by itself predict the loop. Still open: (a) the mechanism by which the backlog-case peer was repaired - its store ended at 61..62 while the leader's was 63..64 at the same applied index 64 and it had applied 61 commands, which is consistent with the peer snapshotting on its own under the shared small SnapshotThreshold and is not isolated; (b) whether the default TrailingLogs (10240) with a matching backlog reproduces the loop, which was never executed; (c) the older registered gaps that this run answered only in prose, because their investigation ids were not resolvable for formal answers. One record inconsistency should be read with this entry: 7465f7b9e6cd44e39e8cbf7e2c45c955-interpretation-0 still reads as refuting the loop for the five-node history, but its Fact was revised (revision 2) and the lineage entry 059c0fbb2e8849188bb09529ad9118a8-interpretation-0 explains that the refutation applied only to the incomplete-partition harness.

knowledge.statement: On accepting an InstallSnapshot, installSnapshot sets lastApplied=req.LastLogIndex and lastSnapshot=(req.LastLogIndex,req.LastLogTerm), restores latest and committed configuration from the snapshot payload, then clears the log store (removeOldLogs) for a monotonic store or compacts it (compactLogs(req.LastLogIndex)) otherwise, and finally sets resp.Success=true. It never calls setLastLog and never truncates a pre-existing log suffix at or above req.LastLogIndex, so lastLogIndex keeps its pre-snapshot value and a stale entry at the snapshot index can remain in the store.
knowledge.conditions: Reached only when the RPC header passes checkRPCHeader, the snapshot version is supported, req.Term >= currentTerm, the snapshot bytes are fully received (n == req.Size) and the FSM restore succeeds.

knowledge.statement: raftState.getLastIndex returns max(lastLogIndex,lastSnapshotIndex) and getLastEntry returns (lastLogIndex,lastLogTerm) whenever lastLogIndex >= lastSnapshotIndex, otherwise (lastSnapshotIndex,lastSnapshotTerm). The comparison is on index only, so when the two sources name the same index with different terms the log-derived term wins. appendEntries uses this as the PrevLogEntry==lastIdx fast path and otherwise reads logs.GetLog(PrevLogEntry); a term mismatch or a missing entry yields Success=false with NoRetryBackoff=true.
knowledge.conditions: Holds for any *Raft whose log and snapshot were written by different ingest paths (NewRaft startup restore, installSnapshot, takeSnapshot, liveBootstrap, dispatchLogs, AppendEntries append, restoreUserSnapshot).

knowledge.statement: In the executed harness, after a successful InstallSnapshot with LastLogIndex=2/LastLogTerm=3, the defect-case node (which had earlier stored a term-2 command at index 2) reported last_log_index=2, last_log_term=2, last_snapshot_index=2, last_snapshot_term=3, get_last_entry_index=2, get_last_entry_term=2, and then rejected the leader's AppendEntries with PrevLogEntry=2/PrevLogTerm=3 (success=false, no_retry_backoff=true, resp_last_log=2). knowledge.statement: On a rejected AppendEntries the leader rewinds the follower's nextIndex to max(min(nextIndex-1, resp.LastLog+1), 1); when that lands on the follower's snapshot boundary L and the leader's own log has been compacted so that L-1 is no longer stored, the rebuild of the request returns ErrLogNotFound, which replicateTo maps to SEND_SNAP. sendLatestSnapshot then ships the current snapshot and, on success, sets nextIndex = meta.Index+1 = L+1, so the following append again carries PrevLogEntry=L. Nothing in the loop removes the follower's stale entry at L or advances the leader's nextIndex past L, so the state that caused the rejection is restored each round.
knowledge.conditions: Applies when the leader's log compaction leaves its first retained index at or above L (for example TrailingLogs=0, or a snapshot taken with more than TrailingLogs entries behind it) and the follower answers PrevLogEntry=L with Success=false because its view of L is a stale earlier-term entry rather than the snapshot's.

knowledge.statement: Standalone correction note (the superseded entries live in an earlier batch and their ids are not resolvable here): The earlier Fact concluded that a legal multi-node history reaches the precondition but the follower does not stay unrepairable, and used that to narrow the leader-side loop. knowledge.statement: compactLogsWithTrailing returns without deleting when lastLogIdx <= trailingLogs and otherwise deletes up to maxLog = min(snapshotIndex, lastLogIdx - trailingLogs), so the leader's retained log begins above the snapshot index when lastLogIdx - trailingLogs >= snapshotIndex at snapshot time. In the same receipt the TrailingLogs=0 case loops (peer applied index pinned at 4, last index 7, thousands of installs) and the (TrailingLogs=10, 20 post-snapshot entries) and (25, 20) cases converge with restores 0 at index 24.
